Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis that affects apple leaves and fruit, especially in cool, wet spring weather.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves
Dark, scabby lesions on fruit surface
Premature leaf yellowing and drop
management: Remove and destroy fallen leaves to reduce fungal spores overwintering
Apply fungicide on a preventive schedule during wet spring conditions
Prune to improve air circulation within the canopy
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where possible
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage wet
Maintain good orchard sanitation each season

Apple___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease (Botryosphaeria obtusa) that can affect apple leaves, fruit, and bark, often entering through wounds or dead wood.
symptoms: Purple-bordered brown spots on leaves ('frog-eye leaf spot')
Rotting, mummified fruit with concentric rings
Cankers on branches
management: Prune out dead or cankered wood during dormant season
Remove mummified fruit from the tree and ground
Apply fungicide following local extension guidance
prevention: Avoid tree stress from drought or poor nutrition
Sanitize pruning tools between cuts
Remove nearby wild or abandoned apple trees that can harbor infection

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A fungal disease requiring both apple/crabapple and juniper/cedar hosts to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface
Small raised structures on the underside of leaves
Premature defoliation in severe cases
management: Apply fungicide in spring when spores are released from cedar galls
Remove nearby juniper/cedar hosts if practical
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars
Increase physical distance between apple trees and juniper/cedar plants

Apple___healthy.description: No visible signs of disease were detected on this apple leaf.
prevention: Continue routine monitoring for early signs of pests or disease
Maintain balanced watering and fertilization

Corn___Common_rust.description: A fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi that produces characteristic rust-colored pustules on corn leaves.
symptoms: Small, cinnamon-brown, raised pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules may turn dark brown to black as leaves mature
management: Apply foliar fungicide if infection is severe and detected early
Monitor fields regularly during humid weather
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which can increase susceptibility

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum, producing long, cigar-shaped lesions on corn leaves.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, gray-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions can merge, causing large areas of dead tissue
management: Apply fungicide when disease pressure is high and weather favors spread
Rotate crops to reduce residue-borne inoculum
prevention: Use resistant hybrids
Till under or manage crop residue after harvest

Corn___healthy.description: No visible signs of disease were detected on this corn leaf.
prevention: Continue routine scouting during the growing season
Maintain proper spacing and nutrition

Potato___Early_blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, common in warm, humid conditions and typically starting on older leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings ('target spot' pattern)
Yellowing of tissue surrounding lesions
Lower/older leaves affected first
management: Apply fungicide at first sign of disease, following label instructions
Remove and dispose of heavily infected foliage
prevention: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants
Avoid overhead watering; water at soil level
Ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow

Potato___Late_blight.description: A historically significant and highly destructive disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, capable of rapidly destroying a crop in favorable conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark green to brown lesions on leaves
White fungal growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid collapse and blackening of foliage
management: Apply appropriate fungicide promptly; late blight can spread very quickly
Remove and destroy infected plants to limit spread
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Avoid excess overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness
Monitor local disease-forecasting networks where available

Potato___healthy.description: No visible signs of disease were detected on this potato leaf.
prevention: Continue routine field scouting
Practice regular crop rotation

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease (Xanthomonas spp.) that affects tomato leaves, stems, and fruit, spreading readily in warm, wet conditions.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots that turn dark brown/black
Spots may have a yellow halo
Fruit can develop raised, scab-like lesions
management: Apply copper-based bactericide where appropriate and permitted
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate crops and avoid overhead irrigation

Tomato___Early_blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani that commonly affects tomato foliage, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings, often on lower leaves first
Yellowing around lesions
Possible stem lesions near the soil line
management: Remove affected lower leaves promptly
Apply fungicide following label guidance
prevention: Stake or cage plants to improve air circulation
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves
Rotate crops annually

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A fast-spreading disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, the same pathogen responsible for potato late blight.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked lesions on leaves
White mold growth on leaf undersides in humid weather
Firm, dark, greasy-looking lesions on fruit
management: Remove and destroy infected plant material immediately
Apply fungicide promptly; disease can spread within days
prevention: Avoid planting near infected potato crops
Improve air circulation and avoid prolonged leaf wetness

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease (Passalora fulva) especially common in greenhouse tomatoes with high humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-purple fuzzy mold on the underside
management: Improve ventilation to reduce humidity
Apply fungicide if conditions favor disease spread
prevention: Space plants adequately
Avoid overhead watering in enclosed/greenhouse settings

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici that produces many small spots, typically starting on lower leaves.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark borders and gray centers
Tiny black fruiting bodies visible within spots
Progressive yellowing and leaf drop from the bottom up
management: Remove infected lower leaves
Apply fungicide as needed, especially in wet seasons
prevention: Rotate crops and avoid planting tomatoes in the same soil yearly
Mulch and avoid overhead watering

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by a tiny arachnid pest rather than a pathogen, common in hot, dry conditions.
symptoms: Fine yellow stippling/speckling on leaves
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves in heavy infestations
Leaves may bronze and dry out
management: Rinse plants with water to dislodge mites
Use insecticidal soap or miticide where appropriate
prevention: Avoid drought stress; mites thrive in dry conditions
Encourage natural predators such as predatory mites

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola producing target-like concentric lesions.
symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric ring patterns, similar to early blight
Can affect leaves, stems, and fruit
management: Apply fungicide following local guidance
Remove severely infected foliage
prevention: Ensure good airflow and avoid leaf wetness
Rotate crops

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A viral disease transmitted primarily by whiteflies, causing significant yield loss in warm climates.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves
Stunted plant growth
Reduced fruit set
management: Control whitefly populations with appropriate methods
Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce virus reservoirs
prevention: Use virus-resistant tomato varieties where available
Use reflective mulches or physical barriers to deter whiteflies

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A highly stable and easily spread virus causing mottled foliage and reduced fruit quality.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion and stunted growth
Occasionally mottled or distorted fruit
management: Remove and destroy infected plants
Disinfect tools and hands, as the virus spreads easily by contact
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed
Avoid handling healthy plants after touching infected ones

Tomato___healthy.description: No visible signs of disease were detected on this tomato leaf.
prevention: Continue routine monitoring
Maintain balanced watering and fertilization
